title: Hypothesis tests, effects, practical significance, A/B guardrails

sections.title: How to use this toolkit
sections.html:
Read Sections 1–4 in order, then use Section 5 to reproduce and communicate the analysis. The core is hypothesis-test logic, a one-mean test, a two-group A/B comparison, effect size, practical significance, and guardrails. The optional bridge is experimental-design vocabulary, multiple comparisons, and Bayes-factor reporting. ANOVA and regression calculations belong to later work, not this session.

The course has no required textbook. The Albright and Winston and Field headings in the outline coverage table are scope cues, not a claim that those chapters have been assigned or read. This chapter is an original synthesis grounded in the open and primary sources actually cited below. It has no stable PDF page numbers: use its numbered section headings for future slide or PNP cross-references after pagination.

You need S05’s distinction between a sample estimate and uncertainty around a population value. Keep four statements separate throughout: observation (what these users did), inference (what a model supports beyond them), assumption (what that inference needs), and recommendation (what to do).

sections.title: The single running case: fictional CedarCart
sections.html:
CedarCart is entirely fictional. It sells household supplies through an app. Its product manager must decide whether to replace the standard checkout screen (A) with a shorter screen (B) for eligible U.S. app users. Each eligible user is randomly assigned once to A or B. The planned analysis uses one row per assigned user, whether or not that user buys. A purchase and a checkout-related complaint are each measured within seven days of assignment.

Decision inputA: standardB: shorterDefinition or proposed rule
Assigned users400400Population of interest: comparable eligible U.S. app users in a future rollout; these 800 are the experiment sample.
Users purchasing160200Primary KPI: purchasers ÷ assigned users. Target: an uplift of at least 8 percentage points.
Users with a complaint832Guardrail: complaint-rate increase must be no more than 1 percentage point.
Illustrative margin assumption—$12 per additional purchaseAn assumption for a rough decision calculation, not an observed profit estimate.
Illustrative rollout cost—$0.60 per exposed userAssumed incremental screen and operating cost.
Illustrative complaint cost—$25 per additional complaintAssumed support cost; it excludes reputational harm.
Separate B-user survey—n=16, xˉ=72, s=8n=16,\ \bar x=72,\ s=8Satisfaction index, 0–100 points; compare with a fixed goal of 70. This is not a second randomized A/B outcome for all 800 users.

The underlying file would require a unique, privacy-protected user_id, assigned variant, assignment timestamp, eligibility flag, seven-day observation-complete flag, purchase indicator, and complaint indicator. The table gives marginal totals, not individual records or the overlap between purchasers and complainants. Before inference, confirm one assignment per user, consistent time windows, no missing outcomes mistaken for zeroes, and that the assignment and recorded group counts match. Even good randomization does not make these 800 users representative of every country, season, or customer type. (Microsoft Research, 2021; The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a).

sections.title: 1. Turn a decision into testable claims
1.1 Specify the comparison, errors, and decision rules
sections.html:
A parameter describes the population of interest. Let pAp_A and pBp_B be future eligible users’ purchase probabilities under A and B. The primary null hypothesis, H0:pB−pA=0H_0:p_B-p_A=0, states no population difference; the alternative, H1:pB−pA≠0H_1:p_B-p_A\ne0, states a difference. A two-sided test permits either improvement or harm. A one-sided alternative, pB−pA>0p_B-p_A>0, is appropriate only if chosen before results and if harm will be handled explicitly. It is not a device for halving an inconvenient p-value afterward. The complaint guardrail is a separate question; purchase success cannot answer it. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b).

Worked decision specification. CedarCart sets a two-sided primary test at α=0.05\alpha=0.05, an 8-percentage-point purchase target, and a maximum 1-percentage-point complaint increase before assignment. Here α\alpha is the long-run probability of a Type I error—rejecting a true null—under the test’s assumptions. If B truly has the same purchase rate, a false positive could trigger a costly rollout. A Type II error means failing to reject when a genuine effect exists; it could cause CedarCart to miss a useful improvement. Power is 1−β1-\beta, the probability of detecting a specified effect when that effect exists. For planning, the team would specify the effect worth detecting and a sample size before collecting data; a small p-value observed afterward is not proof that the study had high power for its business target. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-c).

The test threshold and the rollout threshold do different jobs. For example, a measured uplift of 2 percentage points might be statistically detectable with a huge sample but still miss CedarCart’s 8-point target. Conversely, an estimated 10-point uplift may be too uncertain to establish that the true uplift reaches 8 points. The guardrail is a third, independent reason to withhold rollout.

Write the population claim, error tolerance, worthwhile effect, and harm limit before examining group outcomes. A p-value cannot set those priorities for a manager.

Failure mode: “Fail to reject H0H_0” is not “prove A and B equal.” A weak or noisy test can miss a consequential difference. Nor does a significant randomized result automatically describe users outside the tested population. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b, n.d.-c).

Try it — ungraded. Suppose CedarCart had instead set H1:pB−pA>0H_1:p_B-p_A>0 in advance. If the sample showed B below A, would a small two-sided p-value support that directional claim?

Answer. No. Direction matters. Evidence that B is different because it is worse does not support “B is better.” Report the observed direction, use the prespecified analysis, and examine the harm guardrail.

sections.title: 2. Test one mean without confusing a goal with a control group
2.1 Calculate and interpret a one-sample tt test
sections.html:
Use a one-sample mean test when one quantitative measurement per independent sampled unit is compared with a fixed benchmark. For CedarCart’s separate survey, let μ\mu be the mean satisfaction index among the population represented by surveyed B users. Test H0:μ=70H_0:\mu=70 against H1:μ≠70H_1:\mu\ne70. The index is in points, not percent; 70 is a fixed managerial goal, not the observed mean for A. A tt distribution accounts for estimating population spread with the sample standard deviation ss. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-d).

Worked calculation, with inputs and units. The 16 surveyed B users have xˉ=72\bar x=72 points and s=8s=8 points.

  1. Estimate the standard error of the mean: SE=s/n=8/16=2SE=s/\sqrt n=8/\sqrt{16}=2 points.
  2. Compare the observed mean with the null: t=(xˉ−μ0)/SE=(72−70)/2=1.00t=(\bar x-\mu_0)/SE=(72-70)/2=1.00.
  3. Use df=n−1=15df=n-1=15 degrees of freedom. A two-sided tt probability for ∣t∣≥1.00|t|\ge1.00 is about p=0.333p=0.333.
  4. At α=0.05\alpha=0.05, fail to reject H0H_0. The observed mean is 2 points above the goal, but this sample does not provide strong evidence that the represented population mean differs from 70.
  5. A 95% interval, using a tt critical value of about 2.131, is 72±2.131(2)=[67.74,76.26]72\pm2.131(2)=[67.74,76.26] points. Its inclusion of 70 independently agrees with the two-sided test decision. The standardized observed difference is (72−70)/8=0.25(72-70)/8=0.25 sample standard deviations; this does not tell us whether 2 index points are valuable to customers.

These calculations assume independent respondents and a reasonably appropriate mean model. Sixteen observations warrant inspection for severe skew or influential outliers. More importantly, if dissatisfied users disproportionately ignored the survey, its population claim is restricted by nonresponse; a correct tt calculation cannot repair selection bias. The survey cannot replace the A/B purchase and complaint analysis. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-d; American Statistical Association, 2016).

A benchmark test compares a sample with a fixed value; an A/B test compares outcomes under two assignments. Do not substitute one for the other.

Failure mode: Reporting “B beats A on satisfaction” from these numbers invents an A-group satisfaction measurement. Reporting “the goal is met” because 72>7072>70 ignores the interval and the survey’s coverage.

Try it — ungraded. Keep the same n=16n=16 and s=8s=8, but imagine a survey mean of 68 points. What are the standard error and tt statistic against 70?

Answer. SE=8/16=2SE=8/\sqrt{16}=2 points; t=(68−70)/2=−1.00t=(68-70)/2=-1.00. The minus sign records direction. A two-sided test has the same approximate p-value, 0.333, as for t=+1.00t=+1.00; it still does not establish equality with the goal.

sections.title: 3.1 Work from denominators to a two-proportion result
sections.html:
A proportion is a count of users with an event divided by the number of relevant assigned users. The unit—not a visit or an order—is an assigned user. With independent user assignments and sufficiently many event and non-event counts, a normal-approximation two-proportion zz test compares purchase probabilities. CedarCart has at least 160 purchasers and 200 non-purchasers in each arm, comfortably above the usual small-count warning threshold. If one user appears repeatedly, or post-assignment exclusions differ by arm, this simple test no longer describes the stated design. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-e).

Worked calculation. Write the order of subtraction as B minus A throughout.

  1. Observed rates: p^B=200/400=0.50\hat p_B=200/400=0.50; p^A=160/400=0.40\hat p_A=160/400=0.40. The absolute effect is 0.50−0.40=0.100.50-0.40=0.10, or 10 percentage points. A relative description is 0.10/0.40=25%0.10/0.40=25\% higher than A’s observed rate; “25 percentage points” would be wrong.
  2. Under H0:pB=pAH_0:p_B=p_A, estimate their common probability by pooling successes: p^0=(200+160)/(400+400)=360/800=0.45\hat p_0=(200+160)/(400+400)=360/800=0.45.
  3. Compute the null standard error:
    SE0=p^0(1−p^0)(1/400+1/400)=0.45(0.55)(0.005)≈0.03518.SE_0=\sqrt{\hat p_0(1-\hat p_0)(1/400+1/400)} =\sqrt{0.45(0.55)(0.005)} \approx0.03518.
    This is a fraction of users, equivalent to about 3.518 percentage points.
  4. Standardize the observed difference: z=(0.10−0)/0.03518≈2.843z=(0.10-0)/0.03518\approx2.843.
  5. For a prespecified two-sided test, p=2[1−Φ(2.843)]≈0.0045p=2[1-\Phi(2.843)]\approx0.0045, where Φ\Phi is the standard-normal cumulative probability. Reject H0H_0 at 0.05.
  6. For a 95% interval for the difference, do not reuse the pooled null standard error. Use each arm’s observed rate:
    SECI=0.50(0.50)/400+0.40(0.60)/400=0.001225=0.035.SE_{\mathrm{CI}}=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/400+0.40(0.60)/400} =\sqrt{0.001225}=0.035.
    Thus 0.10±1.96(0.035)=[0.0314,0.1686]0.10\pm1.96(0.035)=[0.0314,0.1686], or approximately 3.14 to 16.86 percentage points.

Observation: 50% of assigned B users and 40% of assigned A users purchased. Inference: under the stated sampling and randomization assumptions, the data are inconsistent with a zero purchase difference; the interval describes plausible differences for comparable eligible users. Not established: that the uplift reaches 8 points—the interval includes values below 8—or that it persists in every future market. The randomized assignment supports a causal interpretation for the tested eligible users if assignment, exposure, measurement, and follow-up operated as stated. The p-value alone neither proves causation nor measures business value. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-e; American Statistical Association, 2016).

Test with the null-based standard error; estimate an unpooled interval for the effect. Report both the absolute difference and its uncertainty.

Failure mode: Dividing purchases by visitors who reached the last checkout step rather than by all assigned eligible users can make B look better merely by excluding users whom B drove away. Changing the denominator changes the KPI and possibly introduces post-assignment bias.

Try it — ungraded. If one purchase in B were found to be a duplicate, what would the corrected B rate and observed B-minus-A effect be? Do not infer a revised p-value from the old one.

Answer. With 199 distinct B purchasers among 400 assigned users, p^B=199/400=0.4975\hat p_B=199/400=0.4975. The corrected absolute effect is 0.4975−0.40=0.09750.4975-0.40=0.0975, or 9.75 percentage points. The pooled estimate and standard error must also be recalculated before retesting.

sections.title: 4. Weigh effect size, business value, and A/B guardrails
4.1 Apply a prespecified decision gate
sections.html:
An effect size expresses magnitude: here, the purchase difference is 10 percentage points, while the complaint difference is another effect on another outcome. Practical significance asks whether those magnitudes matter under CedarCart’s costs and priorities. A guardrail is an outcome that must not degrade beyond an agreed limit. A data-quality diagnostic, such as a group-count check, instead asks whether the experiment can be trusted at all. These are different jobs. Online-experiment practice distinguishes success metrics, guardrails, and data-quality metrics. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-c; Microsoft Research, 2021).

Worked guardrail and business calculation.

  1. Complaint rates are 32/400=0.0832/400=0.08 in B and 8/400=0.028/400=0.02 in A. The observed B-minus-A increase is 0.060.06, or 6 percentage points, against a maximum allowed increase of 1 percentage point.
  2. A descriptive 95% normal interval for that difference uses
    SE=0.08(0.92)/400+0.02(0.98)/400≈0.01526.SE=\sqrt{0.08(0.92)/400+0.02(0.98)/400}\approx0.01526.
    The interval is 0.06±1.96(0.01526)≈[0.0301,0.0899]0.06\pm1.96(0.01526)\approx[0.0301,0.0899]: about 3.01 to 8.99 percentage points. Both groups have at least eight complaint events; this approximation is illustrative, and a lower-count or high-stakes safety analysis merits a method and review chosen in advance. Even the interval’s lower end exceeds the proposed 1-point limit.
  3. For a transparent rough scenario, B has 40 more purchases per 400 assigned users. At an assumed $12 margin each, that is 40($12)=$48040(\$12)=\$480. B’s assumed operating cost is 400($0.60)=$240400(\$0.60)=\$240. Its 24 additional observed complaints imply 24($25)=$60024(\$25)=\$600 of assumed support cost. The scenario’s incremental net is $480−$240−$600=−$360\$480-\$240-\$600=-\$360 per 400 exposed B users, or −$0.90 per B user. This is not an estimated long-run profit interval: the dollar inputs are assumptions, and complaint consequences may be larger.

Recommendation: Do not roll out B as tested. Investigate the complaint types and the user journey; fix the likely cause, validate logging, and plan a new, adequately sized experiment with the same explicit gates. The purchase test is significant and its point estimate exceeds the 8-point target, but its interval does not establish an uplift of at least 8 points. More decisively, the observed complaint increase breaches the guardrail. Do not quietly relax that limit after seeing the result. (American Statistical Association, 2016; Microsoft Research, 2021).

Check assignment balance too: 400/400 matches the planned 1:1 split. This does not prove clean randomization or complete logging; a serious imbalance would prompt investigation of a possible sample-ratio mismatch before trusting either KPI. Privacy-aware review should use access-controlled records and report counts rather than expose user identities. (Microsoft Research, 2021).

Failure mode: Looking at many outcomes, dates, or user segments and presenting only a favorable p-value raises false-positive risk. Prespecify the primary outcome and review plan. Formal multiple-comparison methods are an optional bridge, not permission to conceal adverse outcomes. Bayes factors are another way to compare model evidence, but no Bayes factor is computed from—or implied by—the p-values here. (American Statistical Association, 2016).

Try it — ungraded. Imagine that the same experiment had shown 12 complaints in B rather than 32, with A still at 8. What would the observed complaint-rate increase be, and would its point estimate meet the 1-point limit?

Answer. B’s rate would be 12/400=3%12/400=3\%, versus A’s 8/400=2%8/400=2\%. The increase would be 1 percentage point, exactly the stated maximum, so the point estimate would meet an inclusive “no more than” rule. That alone would not settle rollout: examine uncertainty, measurement quality, the primary effect, and the rule set in advance.

sections.title: 5. Reproduce, check, and report the decision
5.1 Run the same analysis in Excel 365 and SPSS
sections.short: 5.1. Run the same analysis in Ex…
sections.html:
First specify the inputs. On an access-controlled, cleaned user-level file, variant is A or B; purchase and complaint are numeric 0/1; there is exactly one complete seven-day row per eligible assigned user. Rates have units of users per assigned user. Retain a data dictionary, exclusion counts, assignment dates, and a versioned copy of the formulas or syntax. Do not share the user-level file in a slide deck. Excel’s distribution functions and IBM’s T-TEST and CROSSTABS commands are documented by their vendors. (Microsoft, n.d.-a, n.d.-b, n.d.-c; IBM, n.d.).

Excel 365 route. Suppose the validated 800 user rows occupy rows 2:801, with variant in B, purchase in C, and complaint in D. Build an inspectable summary:

CellFormulaExpected result
G2=COUNTIF(B2:B801,"A")400 users
G3=COUNTIF(B2:B801,"B")400 users
H2=COUNTIFS(B2:B801,"A",C2:C801,1)160 purchasers
H3=COUNTIFS(B2:B801,"B",C2:C801,1)200 purchasers
I2=H2/G20.40
I3=H3/G30.50
J2=COUNTIFS(B2:B801,"A",D2:D801,1)8 complaints
J3=COUNTIFS(B2:B801,"B",D2:D801,1)32 complaints

In I4, calculate the purchase difference with =I3-I2 → 0.10. In I5, pool under the null with =(H2+H3)/(G2+G3) → 0.45. In I6, enter =SQRT(I5*(1-I5)*(1/G2+1/G3)) → about 0.035178. In I7, enter =I4/I6 → about 2.842676. In I8, enter =2*(1-NORM.S.DIST(ABS(I7),TRUE)) → about 0.0045. For the effect interval, I9 is =SQRT(I3*(1-I3)/G3+I2*(1-I2)/G2) → 0.035; lower and upper cells are =I4-1.96*I9 and =I4+1.96*I9 → 0.0314, 0.1686. These functions and their arguments are documented by Microsoft. (Microsoft, n.d.-c).

For the separate survey, if its 16 individual index scores occupy L2:L17, verify =COUNT(L2:L17) → 16, =AVERAGE(L2:L17) → 72, and =STDEV.S(L2:L17) → 8 before using =(AVERAGE(L2:L17)-70)/(STDEV.S(L2:L17)/SQRT(COUNT(L2:L17))) → t=1t=1. Then =T.DIST.2T(ABS(1),15) gives approximately 0.333; =T.INV.2T(0.05,15) gives the approximately 2.131 interval multiplier. The aggregate table alone cannot validate the unseen survey scores. (Microsoft, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

SPSS route. After importing and checking the actual 800-row user file, code group as 0=A, 1=B, with numeric purchase and complaint indicators. Run the following on that user-level file, without case weights:

CROSSTABS
  /TABLES=group BY purchase
  /STATISTIC=CHISQ
  /CELLS=COUNT ROW EXPECTED.
CROSSTABS
  /TABLES=group BY complaint
  /STATISTIC=CHISQ
  /CELLS=COUNT ROW EXPECTED.

Check the first table’s group totals of 400 each, purchase counts of 160 and 200, and row purchase percentages of 40% and 50%. With a two-by-two Pearson chi-square test without a continuity correction, z2≈2.8426762≈8.081z^2\approx2.842676^2\approx8.081, so its two-sided significance agrees with the approximately 0.0045 two-proportion zz test. Distinguish the Pearson line from any differently corrected line in the output. The second table must reproduce complaint counts 8 and 32; the business guardrail remains the difference in rates, not just a significance entry. For the separate survey’s individual scores, SPSS’s documented one-sample command is T-TEST TESTVAL=70 /VARIABLES=satisfaction.; inspect nn, mean, standard deviation, tt, dfdf, and the two-sided significance. (IBM, n.d.).

Independently reconcile raw user counts, hand calculations, spreadsheet formulas, and SPSS output before writing the recommendation. If totals differ, stop and trace eligibility, duplicate keys, missing values, and measurement windows.

Failure mode: Excel COUNTIFS treats a blank purchase cell differently from a verified zero. A missing outcome must be investigated, not silently classified as a non-purchase. SPSS and Excel can agree perfectly on a wrongly filtered file.

Try it — ungraded. Your purchase table shows A n=400n=400 and B n=399n=399, but the assignment log records 400 B users. Can you publish the recalculated test?

Answer. Not yet. Locate the missing B record; determine whether it reflects an import error, duplicate handling, eligibility rule, or incomplete follow-up. Document any exclusion and rerun both KPI and guardrail checks on a consistent, defensible denominator. A fresh p-value cannot fix uncertain provenance.

sections.title: Recap
sections.html:
• Frame the stakeholder’s population, decision, KPI, target, harm limit, and testable claim before looking at outcomes.
  • A p-value assesses compatibility with a specified null model; it is neither the probability the null is true nor the size of an effect.
  • For the separate CedarCart survey, t=1.00t=1.00, df=15df=15, and p≈0.333p\approx0.333; its 72-point mean does not establish a population mean different from 70.
  • A and B purchase rates are 40% and 50%. The observed uplift is 10 percentage points, with a 95% interval of about 3.14–16.86 points.
  • The purchase difference is statistically detectable, but its interval does not establish that the true gain reaches the 8-point business target.
  • Complaint rates are 2% and 8%. The 6-point observed increase violates the 1-point guardrail.
  • Under the stated illustrative dollar assumptions, the simple incremental scenario is −$360 per 400 B users; it is not a forecast with quantified uncertainty.
  • Do not roll out B as tested. Investigate complaints and data quality, revise the design, and plan a new experiment.
  • Reconcile user-level denominators and event counts across the source file, Excel, and SPSS; report limitations and the next action alongside the test result.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
• A/B test: A comparison in which eligible units, here users, are assigned to alternative versions.
  • Alternative hypothesis (H1H_1): The population difference a test evaluates as an alternative to the null.
  • Effect size: A measure of a difference’s magnitude, such as a 10-percentage-point purchase uplift.
  • Guardrail: A prespecified limit on an outcome that must not worsen unacceptably.
  • Null hypothesis (H0H_0): The reference population claim used to calculate a test result; here, no purchase-rate difference.
  • Parameter: A value describing a population, such as its purchase probability pBp_B.
  • Percentage point: The arithmetic difference between two percentages; 50% minus 40% is 10 points.
  • Power: The probability that a test detects a specified real effect under its assumptions.
  • p-value: Under a specified null model, the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one.
  • Practical significance: Whether an effect is large enough to matter for a defined decision.
  • Sample-ratio mismatch: A discrepancy between planned and recorded assignment proportions that warrants investigation.
  • Standard error: A measure of how much an estimator would vary across repeated samples under a model.
  • Statistical significance: A result meeting a prespecified test threshold; not a judgment of value.
  • Type I error: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true.
  • Type II error: Failing to reject a null hypothesis when the specified alternative is true.
